doc.title: Chuck Israels interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 11, 2021

title: Concerto Peligroso and holding back the bass and drums
summary: Rowe praises the changing textures of Israels' piece; Israels explains delaying the bass-and-drums time feel for effect.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: And I believe that’s what you’re talking about and I really like what you just said because I struggle with this question of what does music mean, unless it’s descriptive or programmatic and it’s trying to describe something specifically, what does music mean? And I think it means enough if you listen to a Mozart passage and it touches you somehow, like he knew how to use the elements of music and combine them in a way that made me respond. Just like earlier this morning I was listening to your Concerto Peligroso and I was going to get to this a little later but we could go there now because I was really struck by the way that you avoided the common — okay the time’s in the bass and the drums and I’m going to lay everything over that and the bass and drums are going to keep going all the time. Instead you had piano interludes, you had complex unison passages, you had ensemble work where it sounded to me like the bass was laying out and then you brought everybody together. And the texture changed frequently and kept my attention. Was that your intention?

Of course. Yeah. Well I thought the bass and drums playing time feels so good but it feels better if it comes as the lagniappe at the end you know? And when I listen to that I think maybe I held it back a little too long, I’m not sure in terms of the proportions and balance and that. But boy when it comes in you think oh yeah. And that was the effect I was looking for. And you can’t get that effect if you start with that. You have to build some tension and how much of this was an intellectual idea and how much of it was just — I’m not sure what my thought process is all the time, you know, but yes, certainly that was a conscious effort on my part.
